fact: The e-Government Division of the SMART Zambia Institute deployed high-speed internet, with telepresence systems, computers and solar power, at Sinazongwe Town Council in Southern Province, as part of the Government Wide Area Network initiative; no event date is given, so the published date of 26 August 2026 is used.

The connection at Sinazongwe Town Council is expected to let council staff process documents, join virtual meetings and communicate with central government and other local authorities; no national system worked in is named, and no event date is given, so the published date is used.

One council, Sinazongwe Town Council, is reported as given high-speed internet under the Government Wide Area Network initiative, which the article says seeks to connect all 116 councils; no count of councils already connected is given, and the date is the published date.
The deployment at Sinazongwe Town Council was made by the e-Government Division of the SMART Zambia Institute, a state body; the date is the published date.

The article describes the Government Wide Area Network initiative as seeking to connect all 116 councils and government institutions to a secure high-speed backbone; it names no plan document, cost or completion date, and the date is the published date.

Sinazongwe Town Council received high-speed internet, telepresence systems, desktops, laptops and solar power from the SMART Zambia Institute, reported on 26 August 2026 with training of local ICT staff under way.

The article reports that in 2025 the Smart Zambia Institute announced it had linked the country's 116 local authorities to the Government Wide Area Network, 116 of 116 on the institute's own account as relayed by We Are Tech Africa.
The Smart Zambia Institute, the public agency for digital transformation, is reported to have announced in 2025 that it had linked the 116 local authorities to the government's own wide area network.
The linking of the 116 local authorities to the Government Wide Area Network in 2025 is attributed to the Smart Zambia Institute, described as the public agency in charge of digital transformation.

The SMART Zambia e-Government Division announced, in its national coordinator's radio interview of 7 July 2026, that all local authorities and post offices in North-Western Province have been connected through the Government Wide Area Network over fibre.

SMART Zambia says all local authorities in North-Western Province are connected through the Government Wide Area Network as of 7 July 2026; the article gives no number of them and no national count or share of councils connected.

The article says the fibre network in North-Western Province links government offices, schools and health facilities for improved communication and delivery of public services; it names no system that council staff work in over it.

The connection of North-Western Province's local authorities to the Government Wide Area Network is reported as the work of the SMART Zambia e-Government Division, under a digitalisation programme its coordinator says was launched in 2021.
On 7 July 2026 SMART Zambia announced that all local authorities and post offices in North-Western Province had now been connected through the Government Wide Area Network.

Government chief technical officer Kasali Musenge said at a Smart Zambia media brief on 24 March 2026 that all 116 councils have been connected to the government network, 116 of 116, calling phase 1 completed 100 percent.

Smart Zambia's chief technical officer said on 24 March 2026 that all 116 local authorities are connected to the government network, as groundwork for digital service delivery, and that government has provided solar power to all the councils.

Smart Zambia's national coordinator said on 24 March 2026 that data entry into the government's Constituency Development Fund management information system was already under way across councils, with full operation expected by June 2026; the article does not say in so many words that the entry is done at council offices.
The connection of all 116 councils to the government network is reported by Smart Zambia, the government's e-government body, as its own completed phase 1, stated on 24 March 2026.

The article of 25 March 2026 says the digitalisation of local authorities forms part of the national e-government plan, with connecting all 116 councils described as phase 1 and a nationwide e-Council platform planned for 2026; no cost is given.

On 24 March 2026 Smart Zambia said the connection of all 116 councils to the government network was complete, that a Constituency Development Fund system was in data entry across councils, and that eight councils would begin an e-Council proof of concept with demonstration by 19 June 2026.

Smart Zambia's national coordinator Percy Chinyama listed connecting all 116 local authorities to the government network among the institute's progress over 2021 to 2025, 116 of 116 on his account to the state news agency; the briefing is undated, so the published date is used.
The Smart Zambia Institute says it has connected all 116 local authorities to the government network; the briefing is undated, so the published date is used.

The connection of the 116 local authorities to the government network is reported by the Smart Zambia Institute as its own work over 2021 to 2025; the briefing is undated, so the published date is used.

The article reports Bwalya and Mulundano's 2023 survey of local authorities as finding that all of them undertook e-procurement on the Zambia Public Procurement Authority's e-GP platform, while a majority (70%) reported constraints including unstable internet connectivity and limited ICT infrastructure; it does not say from where the councils work or who provides the connection, and gives no survey date, so the cited study's year is used.

The National Electronic Government Plan 2023-2026 says Government will expand the Government Wide Area Network to cover the 116 district administrative centres and local authorities, and its matrix lists deploying GWAN in public institutions and local authorities (K500 million) and metro networks in all local authorities (targets of 57 and 57; K95.86 million).

The plan names the Electronic Government Division, with the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, internet service providers, the finance ministry and ZICTA, as implementers of GWAN deployment in public institutions and local authorities.
The plan says it will depend largely on domestic financing through annual national budget allocations, with public-private partnerships, grants and concessional loans as part of the funding.

The plan says that at December 2022 only 263 of 15,600 targeted national sites were connected to the GWAN, with expansion earmarked mostly for district administrative centres, local authorities and border posts; its table has a row for local authorities connected, whose figure cannot be read from the parsed text.

The finance minister told the National Assembly that 93 local authorities had so far been connected to the Government Wide Area Network, in a paragraph that counts 116 councils (93 of 116), alongside 79 district administration offices and 29 schools, 438 sites cumulatively.
The budget address says Government continued to roll out the Government Wide Area Network to public institutions and had connected 93 local authorities to it.
The budget address gives the purpose of connecting 93 local authorities to the Government Wide Area Network only as improving public service delivery; no use is named.
The finance minister describes the roll-out of the Government Wide Area Network to local authorities as Government's own.

SMART Zambia's principal ICT officer for Western Province said GWAN works were complete at 12 sites, six of them town councils (Mitete, Limulunga, Sioma, Mwandi, Mulobezi, Nalolo) and six district commissioners' offices, but that the network could not be fully used until ZAMTEL and others finished the last-mile connections.

The officer said completing the last-mile connections with ZAMTEL would enable the GWAN at the 12 Western Province sites, six town councils among them, to be fully utilised; no use over it is reported.
The GWAN works at Western Province town councils are reported by SMART Zambia's own provincial ICT officer, with the state-owned ZAMTEL to supply the last-mile links.

An International Growth Centre policy brief says most local councils still run on manual systems and lists lack of appropriate ICT infrastructure, such as internet connectivity and storage space, among the challenges to councils taking up technology; it gives no count of councils.

The National Electronic Government Plan's Table 2 gives 2 local authorities connected to the Government Wide Area Network against a national target of 116, as at December 2022 (beside 10 of 116 district administration offices and 263 of 15,600 targeted sites); the percentage is computed from the plan's two figures, which the plan itself does not state as a share.
The plan counts 2 local authorities as sites connected to the Government Wide Area Network, the government's own network deployed by the state, as at December 2022.

The Government Wide Area Network is deployed by the Electronic Government Division in the Office of the President, which the plan names with the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, the Ministry of Finance, ZICTA and internet service providers as implementers of its extension; dated to the plan's publication.

The National Electronic Government Plan 2023-2026 commits to expanding the Government Wide Area Network to the 116 district administrative centres and local authorities, and its costed matrix carries deployment to 497 further sites at ZMW 500,000,000 and metro networks in 114 local authorities at ZMW 95,860,000.

The plan says its implementation, the network's extension included, shall depend largely on domestic financing through annual national budget allocations, with public-private partnerships, grants and concessional loans as part of the funding; it states an intention, not a budget line for local authority connections.
